1	You are adjudicating disagreements between a benchmark case's answer key and an independent expert's blind solution. For each flagged item, rule whether the key's answer is uniquely defensible from the evidence (key-uniquely-defensible), whether two answers are defensible (ambiguous), or whether the key is wrong (key-wrong). If not uniquely defensible, propose the smallest change to the case evidence or the key that would make exactly one answer defensible.
2	
3	Answer semantics:
4	- hypothesis: "supported" = the evidence, taken together, supports the claim more than its rivals; "contradicted" = the evidence counts against it; "unknown" = the evidence does not discriminate, so the claim is live but unestablished.
5	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.
6	- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.
7	- sufficiency (item SUFF): is the evidence sufficient to commit to the action you rank highest, where that action is substantive rather than merely evidence-gathering? "sufficient" or "insufficient". Concluding that no intervention is warranted counts as a substantive decision.
8	- Items with asOfStage set must be answered using only evidence whose stage is at or before that stage.
9	
10	Truth convention: expected answers are what a careful analyst concludes after reading the initial file plus the optimal read path (at most three catalogue items); for INCOMPLETE and NOCONC cases, what the whole catalogue supports.

296	CASE OD2-HO-CONFOUND-1 (CONFOUND, organizational): Remote promotion gap at Fenwright Data Services
297	Setting: Fenwright Data Services is a fictional data-services company with about 1,100 employees across two offices, Larkhaven and Calderbrook, plus a fully remote workforce. Promotions are decided in one annual cycle: managers nominate and a Promotion Committee of directors approves or defers nominations. The FY2026 cycle closed in September 2026, and the People Analytics dashboard shows remote employees promoted at less than half the rate of office-based employees.
298	Presenting request: The COO has asked the People team to confirm by Friday that proximity bias explains the remote promotion gap, so the executive team can announce a rule that employees must work from an office at least three days a week to be considered for promotion. You have been asked to say what is driving the gap and what the company should do.
299	INITIAL EVIDENCE
300	E1 [stage S1] People Analytics promotion dashboard (system-record): Promotion dashboard, FY2026 cycle (census 31 Aug 2026; decisions effective 1 Oct 2026). Promotion rate = promotions divided by headcount at census. Office-based (including hybrid): 122 of 760 (16.1%). Remote: 26 of 340 (7.6%). By job family: Engineering, office 61/380 (16.1%), remote 14/170 (8.2%). Customer Operations, office 33/220 (15.0%), remote 7/110 (6.4%). Sales & Account Management, office 28/160 (17.5%), remote 5/60 (8.3%). Automated dashboard flag: 'Remote promotion rate below office rate in every job family.'
301	E2 [stage S1] Email from Danica Ferrol, Chief Operating Officer, to the executive team (leadership-account): Subject: Remote promotion gap. 'The dashboard could not be clearer. Remote staff are promoted at under half the office rate, in every job family. This is proximity bias, plain and simple: people who aren't in the room don't get seen. I propose that from the FY2027 cycle, anyone who wants to be considered for promotion works from an office at least three days a week. I know roughly 180 of our remote people live more than 150 km from Larkhaven or Calderbrook and were hired on home-based contracts, but if they want to progress they need to be visible. Can the People team confirm the diagnosis by Friday so we can announce?'
302	E3 [stage S1] HR business partner interview notes, 15 Oct 2026 (manager-account): Engineering manager (Larkhaven, team of 11, 5 remote): 'When an urgent client escalation comes in I'll usually hand it to whoever's sitting near me. It's quicker. I suppose that's the kind of work that gets noticed at promotion time.' Customer Operations manager (Calderbrook, team of 14, 6 remote): 'None of my remote people were put forward this year. Honestly, they're solid. Most of them haven't been with us long, and I didn't have a remote person I could make a case for yet.' Neither manager could say how many stretch assignments each team member had received this year.
303	E4 [stage S1] Fenwright Promotion Policy v4 (effective January 2024), section 3 (document): Section 3, Eligibility. 3.1 To be nominated in an annual cycle, an employee must have at least 18 months in their current level at the census date and a most recent performance rating of 'Meets' or above. 3.2 Managers nominate. The Promotion Committee approves or defers each nomination. 3.3 Exception nominations for employees with under 18 months in level require a director's written justification and are expected to be rare. 3.4 Work location is recorded on the nomination packet for administrative purposes.
304	E5 [stage S1] Engagement pulse survey, June 2026 (anonymous-staff-survey): Response rate: remote 71%, office-based 64%. 'I understand what I need to do to be promoted here': agree, remote 41%, office-based 58%. 'Senior leaders are aware of my work': agree, remote 33%, office-based 47%. 'My manager supports my career development': agree, remote 72%, office-based 70%. 'I have the tools I need to do my job well': agree, remote 81%, office-based 79%. Results are reported by work arrangement only; no breakdown by tenure is available in the survey tool.
305	CATALOGUE (full contents)
306	C1 [stage S1] Promotion nominations and outcomes by time in current level and work arrangement, FY2026 cycle - People Analytics extract from HRIS and promotion-workflow records (system-record): Census 31 Aug 2026. Eligible = 18+ months in current level. Office-based: eligible 560, nominated 160 (28.6%), approved 118 (73.8% of nominees; 21.1% of eligible). Not eligible 200, exception nominations 6, approved 4 (2.0%). Remote: eligible 110, nominated 31 (28.2%), approved 22 (71.0% of nominees; 20.0% of eligible). Not eligible 230, exception nominations 6, approved 4 (1.7%). Share of headcount eligible: office 73.7%, remote 32.4%. Applying office within-band rates to the remote eligibility mix gives an expected remote rate of 8.2%, against the observed 7.6%. Analyst note: the eligible-band difference of 1.1 points rests on 110 remote employees. It could be chance, and these data cannot rule out a true difference of several points in either direction.
307	C2 [stage S1] Hiring, transfer and voluntary exit records by work arrangement, January 2024 to August 2026 - HRIS workforce records (system-record): Remote hiring was opened to all roles in July 2024. Before that, remote work required an individual exception. Remote employees at 31 Aug 2026: 340. Start dates: before July 2024, 61; July 2024 to February 2025, 64; March 2025 to August 2026, 215. Office-based employees at 31 Aug 2026: 760, of whom 120 started in March 2025 or later. Voluntary exits in the 12 months to 31 Aug 2026: remote 31 (10.9% of average headcount 285); office-based 88 (11.6% of average headcount 757). First-year voluntary exit rate: remote 14.2%, office-based 15.0%. Transfers between arrangements since July 2024: 22 office-to-remote, 3 remote-to-office.
308	C3 [stage S1] Performance rating distribution by work arrangement, 2026 mid-year review - HRIS performance module (system-record): Five-point scale. Among rated employees: 'Meets' or above, remote 87%, office-based 88%. 'Exceeds' or above, remote 24%, office-based 27%. 'Below' or lower, remote 4%, office-based 3%. Employees with under six months' service at the review date are not rated: remote 92, office-based 41. Ratings are entered by line managers and moderated within each job family. No calibration adjustment by work arrangement was recorded.
309	C4 [stage S1] Promotion Committee calibration minutes, FY2026 cycle - Promotion Committee secretary (document): The committee of six directors met 9 to 11 September 2026 and reviewed 203 nominations, including 12 exception nominations. 148 were approved and 55 were not approved, 14 of them recorded as 'insufficient evidence of scope'. Packets include the manager's case, rating history, level, time in level and work location. Reasons are recorded per case, but outcomes are not tallied by location. One director commented that 'remote cases tended to be thinner on cross-team examples'. The chair noted that this had not been checked.
310	C5 [stage S1] Promotion nomination form template and manager guidance, 2026 - People team intranet (document): The nomination form has four sections: scope evidence, impact examples, peer feedback and a readiness statement. The guidance asks managers to 'include at least two cross-team examples' and to keep the case under 1,200 words. Level, time in level, latest rating and work location are filled in automatically from HRIS. The guidance has not changed since the 2024 cycle apart from a new deadline date.
311	C6 [stage S1] Office badge-access records for office-based staff, January to August 2026 - Facilities access-control system (log): Office-based staff averaged 3.2 badge days per week (Larkhaven 3.4, Calderbrook 2.9). 14% of hybrid staff averaged fewer than one badge day per week. Attendance peaks on Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Records cover only employees assigned to an office and include no remote staff. The extract was not linked to promotion, rating or nomination data.
312	C7 [stage S1] Base-pay position within salary band by work arrangement, 2026 pay review - Reward team (financial-record): Median compa-ratio (base pay divided by band midpoint): remote 0.97, office-based 0.99. Under the offer guidelines, remote new hires since 2025 were placed at 0.95 on average. Pay is not location-adjusted within the country. The 2026 merit budget was 3.5% for both groups. The review found no band breaches and made no recommendations on work arrangement.
313	C8 [stage S1] Free-text comments from remote respondents, June 2026 engagement pulse - Survey vendor export (214 comments; selection shown) (anonymous-staff-survey): 'You have to be in Larkhaven to get noticed.' 'My manager is great but the directors have never met me.' 'Nobody told me when I was hired that I couldn't go for promotion until I'd been here a year and a half.' 'Office people get the fun client fires.' 'Remote has been fine for my career so far.' 'Visibility is a problem; I'm not sure promotions are.' The selection was chosen by the People team to illustrate themes and is not weighted by frequency.
314	C9 [stage S1] Interview with the Promotion Committee chair, 20 October 2026 - Director of Engineering (office-based), committee chair (leadership-account): 'We judge the case, not the postcode. Location is on the packet because payroll needs it, and nobody looks at it. If remote people aren't getting through, it's because they aren't being nominated, so talk to managers.' When asked for figures, the chair said the committee does not keep approval rates by location. 'I'd be surprised if there's any difference at our stage, but I haven't looked.'
315	C10 [stage S1] Industry report on promotion outcomes for remote workers, 2026 - Northgrid Insights, workplace-analytics vendor (external-data): Across 41 participating employers (anonymised), fully remote employees were promoted at 0.69 times the rate of office-based peers. The report attributes the gap to 'visibility deficits' and markets a visibility-coaching product. Methodology note: rates are raw promotions divided by headcount, with no adjustment for tenure, level or role. Participating employers self-selected, and Fenwright is not among them.
316	C11 [stage S1] Learning-platform course completions by work arrangement, January to August 2026 - Learning management system (telemetry): Average course completions per employee: remote 6.1, office-based 4.8. Mandatory compliance modules: 97% completion in both groups. Enrolment in the leadership-track programme: remote 9%, office-based 11%. Completion data are not linked to promotion records. The platform team notes that onboarding courses inflate completion counts for recent joiners.
317	C12 [stage S1] Reporting lines and manager span of control by work arrangement - HRIS organisation data (system-record): Of 340 remote employees, 221 (65%) report to office-based managers and 119 to remote managers. Average span of control: office-based managers 8.1 direct reports, remote managers 7.6. Average number of manager changes in the past 12 months: remote 0.3, office-based 0.3. This extract does not include promotion, nomination or rating outcomes by manager location.
318	C13 [stage S1] Project staffing records by work arrangement, January to August 2026 - Project staffing system export (system-record): Records project codes and hours booked per employee. Average concurrent projects: remote 2.3, office-based 2.4. The 'role on project' field, intended to flag lead or stretch roles, is blank on 71% of records. Client-escalation work is booked to a general support code and is not attributed to individuals. People Analytics comment: 'This system cannot tell us who received stretch or high-visibility work.'
319	C14 [stage S1] FY2025 promotion cycle summary by work arrangement - People Analytics annual report, October 2025 (prior-report): FY2025 cycle, census 31 Aug 2025. Promotion rate = promotions divided by headcount at census. Office-based: 113 of 731 (15.5%). Remote: 17 of 181 (9.4%). rulings.explanation: R1 claims that working remotely causes a lower chance of promotion. The raw link is real and repeats across years: 7.6% vs 16.1% in E1, and 9.4% vs 15.5% in C14. 'Contradicted' would need evidence that counts against the link itself, as C2 does for R3, where there is no association at all. C1 does not do that. Within each band the remaining differences still point in the claimed direction: 20.0% vs 21.1% among eligible staff and 1.7% vs 2.0% among the rest. The analyst note also says the data cannot rule out a true difference of several points in either direction. So C1 counts against location explaining the 8.5-point gap, not against any causal effect existing. That matches 'association-only' (they co-occur, causation not established). rulings.fix: None needed. Optionally, add one sentence to the C1 analyst note: 'The data neither show nor exclude a small direct effect of location.' This would make the R1 reading explicit.

rulings.explanation: H1 is a claim about where the gap comes from: favouritism by managers and the Promotion Committee. C1 tests both stages directly. Because C1 discriminates between H1 and H2, 'unknown' does not fit. The evidence pointing the other way is weak. E3 and C4 are anecdotes, and C4's comment was explicitly unchecked. C10 uses unadjusted vendor figures. The small, uncertain residual among eligible staff might allow a minor favouritism effect, but it cannot rescue H1's actual claim that favouritism produces the gap. A careful analyst would mark H1 as contradicted.

E5 is not broken down by tenure, so the understanding gap may simply reflect how recently many remote staff joined. C8 is a hand-picked selection of comments. A4 is reasonable but not among the best actions, so 'acceptable' is correct and 'preferred' overstates it.
rulings.fix: None needed. Optionally, reword A4's rationale to note that briefings cannot change eligibility and so do not address the gap or the pending decision.
